Family Health

Lower back pain in women: patterns, relief and assessment

Updated: November 12, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Lower back pain can start after a busy day or arrive without an obvious trigger. Muscles, joints, nerves and pelvic conditions can produce overlapping symptoms. The useful first step is to describe the pattern and check warning signs, rather than assuming that every ache comes from housework, hormones or a damaged disc.

Start with what changes the pain

Notice where the pain begins, whether it travels into a buttock or leg, and what happens with walking, lifting, sitting or rest. Record when it started and which tasks have become difficult. Pain after repeated lifting or an unfamiliar effort may fit a strain, but that history does not prove the diagnosis.

Also note period timing, unusual bleeding, pain during sex, bowel or urinary symptoms and pregnancy possibility. The side of the ache alone cannot identify an ovary, kidney or nerve problem. More than one condition can coexist, so a familiar menstrual pattern should not explain away a new neurological symptom.

Strains and changes in the spine

A strain affects a muscle or tendon; a sprain affects a ligament supporting the spine. Sudden or repeated loading can contribute, sometimes with stiffness or muscle spasm. In other cases, no single injured structure can be identified. Being unable to name an exact cause does not mean the pain is imaginary.

Discs act as cushions between spinal bones. They change with age, and disc degeneration, joint changes or a narrowed spinal canal may contribute to symptoms in some people. Age or a phrase in a scan report is not enough to decide what hurts or whether an operation is needed. The findings must fit the symptoms and examination.

Sciatica and a herniated disc are related but different

Sciatica describes symptoms from an irritated or compressed sciatic nerve. Pain commonly travels from a buttock down the back of one leg, sometimes to the foot, with burning, tingling, numbness or weakness. The leg pain may be more prominent than the backache. Pain confined to the back is less suggestive of sciatica.

A herniated or slipped disc means some of its softer material bulges outward and may irritate nearby nerves. Not every disc bulge causes symptoms, and sciatica has other possible causes. Many episodes improve without surgery. Report new weakness or worsening loss of sensation promptly, and use emergency care for the warning signs below.

Menstrual timing is a clue, not a diagnosis

Period cramps can spread into the lower back or thighs around the start of bleeding. PMS involves a recurring combination of physical and emotional symptoms before a period, such as bloating, fatigue, headaches, appetite changes or irritability, which usually ease after bleeding begins. Keep a diary over two cycles if possible, including days without symptoms. Do not postpone help to finish it.

PMDD involves a particular severe premenstrual symptom pattern with marked mood symptoms and disruption of daily life; backache alone does not establish it. Endometriosis, in which tissue similar to the uterine lining grows elsewhere, can cause back or pelvic pain, painful periods, sex or bowel/urinary pain, and sometimes difficulty conceiving. Pain outside bleeding days is possible. Disabling, changing or persistent symptoms deserve assessment rather than a label of normal period pain.

Pregnancy changes the advice

Backache can begin early in pregnancy as supporting tissues change, and later load and balance changes can contribute. There is no single month when it must start, and backache cannot confirm pregnancy. Discuss new or troubling pain with your maternity team; pregnancy-specific positioning and labour advice need their own care plan.

Seek urgent maternity advice for back pain in the second or third trimester, or pain with fever, vaginal bleeding, painful urination or pain in the side below the ribs. Neurological warning signs still need emergency assessment during pregnancy. For pregnancy-specific guidance, see BeMama’s back pain and labour guide: https://bemamas.com/pregnancy/back-pain-and-labour-signs-relief/

Recognise an emergency before trying home care

With back pain, seek emergency assessment for new altered feeling around the genitals or anus, difficulty passing urine, loss of bladder or bowel control, or new sexual sensation or function changes. Pain, numbness, tingling or weakness affecting both legs also needs emergency assessment, as does new loss of feeling in one or both legs. Do not wait for all these signs or complete incontinence.

Back pain after a serious accident, or accompanied by chest pain, also needs emergency care. Do not drive yourself. These warnings may indicate a condition needing rapid investigation rather than an ordinary strain. A previous diagnosis of sciatica or pelvic pain does not make new nerve or bladder symptoms safe to monitor at home.

Keep everyday movement manageable

If there are no warning signs and the pain is suitable for self-care, continue gentle daily activity within your ability. Short walks and regular changes of position can be easier than one long effort. Avoid spending long periods in bed. Reduce an aggravating load temporarily, then build activity back up with advice if needed.

There is no universally perfect sitting posture. Try a comfortable supported chair, keep your feet supported and change position regularly. Break up repetitive tasks and ask for help with bulky loads. Exercise should be chosen for your abilities and symptoms; stop an activity that makes the pain worse and seek advice about adapting it.

Warmth, cold and pillows can improve comfort

A wrapped cold pack may help discomfort, while wrapped warmth or a comfortably warm bath may ease stiffness or spasm. Protect your skin and stop if uncomfortable. These are ways to manage symptoms, not proof that the cause has healed or a reason to delay assessment.

For rest, try a pillow under the knees when lying on your back, or between the knees when lying on your side, if that feels better. A pillow does not cure a disc problem or guarantee recovery. Choose a position that lets you relax; pregnancy and other health conditions may require different positioning advice.

Check medicines for the pain and for your health

An anti-inflammatory medicine such as ibuprofen may suit some adults with ordinary low back pain, but the choice depends on stomach, kidney, heart and other health risks and your existing medicines. Ask a pharmacist or clinician and follow the agreed instructions. If prescribed, use the lowest effective dose for the shortest needed period. Paracetamol alone is not generally recommended for ordinary low back pain; advice for pregnancy or pelvic pain can differ.

Check before taking an NSAID if pregnant or possibly pregnant. FDA advises avoiding these medicines from 20 weeks unless specifically directed because of fetal kidney and low-amniotic-fluid risks. Prescribed low-dose aspirin is a separate situation: do not stop it on your own. Hormonal treatment or an antidepressant may have a role for a diagnosed menstrual or mood condition, but neither should be started simply because the lower back hurts. Endometriosis care may include pain treatment, suitable hormones or selected surgery, taking symptoms and fertility plans into account; surgery is not a guaranteed cure.

An assessment should lead to a practical plan

Get urgent medical advice for pain with fever, shivering or feeling unwell, sudden severe pain or rapid worsening. Arrange review if pain interferes with daily life, persists for a few weeks despite self-care, recurs, or occurs with unexplained weight loss or night/rest pain. An injury, new leg symptoms or severe abdominal or pelvic symptoms also changes the assessment; do not wait for a fixed one-week deadline.

A clinician may examine movement, leg strength, reflexes and sensation, and investigate pelvic or urinary clues separately. Routine spinal imaging is often unnecessary; a specialist considers it when the result would change care. Physiotherapy, exercise and sometimes combined physical and psychological support can help restore function. Injections and surgery are selective: an epidural may be considered for acute severe sciatica, and decompression when nonoperative treatment has not improved pain or function and imaging fits the symptoms. Neither is a routine next step for every backache.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Record pain location, leg symptoms, activity limits and relevant cycle or urinary changes.

Agree on suitable relief, realistic activity goals and when to reassess persistent symptoms.

Act on urgent or emergency changes before trying another exercise, medicine or tracking entry.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help organise symptom patterns, medicine questions and follow-up plans. It cannot identify the source of back pain, interpret a scan or rule out a spinal or pregnancy emergency.

When to seek help

Seek emergency care for new saddle-area sensation changes, bladder/bowel dysfunction, sexual sensation changes or the significant leg warning signs described above, or back pain after a serious accident or with chest pain. Sudden severe or rapidly worsening pain and fever or marked illness need urgent advice. Check medicine suitability, especially in pregnancy.

Evidence notes updated: November 12, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Describe movement and leg symptoms alongside menstrual, urinary and pelvic changes.
  • A disc finding or the timing of an ache cannot establish its cause on its own.
  • Keep activity manageable and use comfort measures without expecting a guaranteed cure.
  • Choose medicines and further treatment for the assessed problem and your individual risks.
  • New saddle, bladder, bowel or significant leg symptoms can require emergency care.

Frequently asked questions

What can cause severe lower back pain?

A strain, nerve irritation, disc or joint problem and other conditions can cause pain. Severity alone cannot identify the cause. Sudden severe or rapidly worsening pain needs urgent advice; new nerve or bladder/bowel warning signs need emergency assessment.

Can pregnancy cause lower back pain?

Yes, including early pregnancy, but an ache cannot diagnose pregnancy or exclude another problem. New or concerning pain needs maternity advice, with emergency care for neurological warning signs.

Will a pillow under my knees cure it?

It may make resting more comfortable for some people. A pillow between the knees while side-lying is another option. Neither corrects every cause or replaces assessment when symptoms persist or change.

When should I see a specialist?

Start with appropriate medical assessment when symptoms limit activity, persist or recur. The findings guide referral; you do not need to wait a fixed week. New saddle sensation, bladder/bowel changes or other emergency signs require immediate care rather than a routine specialist appointment.

Does pain before a period mean PMS or PMDD?

Timing is useful, but back pain alone does not diagnose either condition. Record physical and mood symptoms and their impact across the cycle, and seek assessment for disabling or changed symptoms.

Does a slipped disc always need surgery?

No. Some disc bulges cause no symptoms, and many symptomatic episodes improve without surgery. An operation is considered for particular clinical findings, not simply because a scan mentions a disc.

Should I stop moving until the pain disappears?

Usually not for uncomplicated back pain. Use manageable activity and avoid prolonged bed rest, adjusting tasks that aggravate symptoms. Follow individualized advice after injury or when warning signs or another condition is present.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
